The story: programmer Kazuhisa Hashimoto was porting Gradius from arcade to NES and found it too hard to get through during his own testing/debugging, so he built in a cheat that instantly gave full power-ups when entered — that's the origin of the up-up-down-down-left-right-left-right-B-A(-select-start) sequence. It later became far more famous through **Contra** (1988), where entering it gave you 30 lives instead of 3, which is why a lot of English-speaking players call it the "Contra Code" even though Gradius came first.

"Konami Command") is a special combination of buttons that appears in several Konami games. It was widely popularized due to its inclusion in the original Contra video game, where it allowed the player to obtain 30 free lives. Since it was first revealed, the code has become part of popular culture in general, even appearing in many non-Konami games and diverse media, such as clothing, advertisements and non-gaming related software. ... 

The code was first used in the 1986 release of Gradius for the Nintendo Entertainment System but was popularized among North American players in the NES version of Contra, for which it was also dubbed both the "Contra Code" and "30 Lives Code", because of its nearly necessary use in the game.

The Konami Code was created by Kazuhisa Hashimoto, who was developing the home port of the 1985 arcade game Gradius, a horizontal scrolling shooter released on the NES in 1986. Finding the game too difficult to play through during testing, he created a cheat code to give the player a full set of power-ups (normally attained gradually throughout the game). The code was still present in the released version after Hashimoto forgot to remove it. Players discovered and shared the code. The Konami Code was thus included in the series' other sequels and spin-offs.

content.title: The Secret Origin of Cheat Codes Nobody Tells You About
content.text:
It wasn’t until years later, ... Kazuhisa Hashimoto into the NES port of Gradius because he found his own build too difficult to get through during debugging....

After that I tried it on basically every NES game I got my hands on, half expecting it to do something every time. Sometimes it worked. Sometimes nothing happened and I moved on without wondering why. It wasn’t until years later, going back through the actual history of cheat codes, that I found out the sequence had a name at all: the Konami Code, built by programmer Kazuhisa Hashimoto into the NES port of Gradius because he found his own build too difficult to get through during debugging. It shipped in Contra too, and in dozens of other titles, which is exactly why a kid mashing buttons on unrelated games kept half expecting it to do something. It wasn’t random luck that it sometimes worked. It was one code, quietly reused across an entire console’s library, by developers who all had the same problem Hashimoto did. 

None of this came from a website, because there was no website.

None of this ever really stopped. The developer who built a shortcut into Gradius so he could survive his own game and the person who builds a staging environment shortcut today so a QA team doesn’t have to click through ten screens to test one state are running the exact same instinct forty years apart. The cheat code was never a novelty bolted onto a finished game. It was always the same job, it just used to be a secret, and now it has a name. content.text:
It’s a sequence so ingrained in the collective memory of gamers that even non-gamers might hum it: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A, Start. The Konami Code. It’s more than just a string of button presses; it’s a cultural ...

It’s a sequence so ingrained in the collective memory of gamers that even non-gamers might hum it: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A, Start. The Konami Code. It’s more than just a string of button presses; it’s a cultural touchstone, a secret handshake for a generation, and a testament to how a little bit of programmer ingenuity can echo through decades. But where did this iconic sequence even come from? It wasn't born out of a desire for world domination or to make games impossibly easy from the get-go. The story, as it often goes with these things, is a bit more practical, and frankly, a lot more human. 

Back in the day, when games were being developed for systems like the Nintendo Entertainment System, debugging was a real headache. Programmers needed ways to test their creations thoroughly, and sometimes, that meant giving themselves a little edge. Kazuhisa Hashimoto, the genius behind the code, was working on the NES version of Gradius.

Interestingly, the original Gradius wasn't the first place it appeared in a Konami game, but it was the first to feature this specific sequence. The NES version of Gradius would grant the player all power-ups (except for a few specific ones) when the code was entered while paused. It was a lifesaver for testing, and it worked. From there, it migrated to other Konami titles, most famously to Contra on the NES, where it famously gifted players a whopping 30 lives instead of the usual three. Suddenly, that notoriously tough shooter felt a little more approachable. What’s fascinating is how the code evolved.

content.title: Cheating Wonders: A Brief History of the Konami Code
content.text:
The code first appeared in the NES version of game developer Konami’s classic space-shooter Gradius in 1986. The developer who was converting the game from its arcade version to the console version, Kazuhisa Hashimoto, couldn’t actually beat the game because it was too hard, so he created what would come to be known as the Konami Code, to give himself a cheat that tricked out his little ship with all the game’s power-ups. As the story goes, he simply forgot to take it out of the code before the NES version was released.
(Photo: Kevin Simpson/Flickr)
Hashimoto’s code would go on to be included in each subsequent Gradius sequel and franchise expansion, but it was the code’s inclusion in the 1988 NES version of ultra-macho shoot-em-up Contra that solidified its place in the cultural consciousness.

content.title: Image Credits:Konami
content.text:
Image Credits:Konami

‘Konami Code’ creator Kazuhisa Hashimoto has died

Up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A, then start. Sound familiar? The Konami Code, as this sequence came to be known, is one of the most recognizable artifacts of an earlier era of gaming. Kazuhisa Hashimoto, its creator, has used up the last of his 30 lives.

Hashimoto was a programmer at Konami, and created the code during the development of one of Konami’s best-known games of the 8-bit era: Gradius. Anyone who played it will remember the crushing difficulty of this iconic side-scrolling shooter.

Even the developers, it turns out, found it a bit of a hassle to get through repeatedly for testing purposes. That’s why during the porting process from arcade to NES, Hashimoto made himself a bit of a shortcut to make things a bit easier for himself.

He created a special command that would award the player the most crucial items for surviving the game’s challenges. 

The sequence to activate it needed to be easy for him to remember during his many playthroughs, but extremely unlikely for a player to input by accident. And so he settled on the well-known “up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A” — after which is usually appended “start,” since the code is often entered while paused or at the title screen.

Fate intervened here and the code, which was meant to be removed before the team wrapped up, was forgotten about and ended up in the shipping product. Somehow word got out about the code (who knows how such things transpired in the ’80s — probably it was published in Nintendo Power) and, given the extreme difficulty of the game, its necessity led to the code being adopted by pretty much everyone who bought Gradius.

And so millions of kids who grew up in the ’80s and ’90s learned the Konami Code by heart, though its effects differed from game to game, it generally made things considerably easier.
